title: Zero-knowledge proof of AI inference with FlashProve
excerpt: FlashProve lets an AI provider prove a model’s answer without revealing its weights, using a GPU-generated proof verified on a CPU in seconds.
body:
A recent commit to the FlashProve repository shows the prototype can generate a zero-knowledge proof for a full-size Llama 4 Maverick model on a single NVIDIA H100. The prover reaches roughly 110 tokens / second of pre-fill when handling 24 requests per batch. That performance number comes straight from the README and demonstrates the system is not just a toy; it can handle a 1,024-token context window at production-scale throughput.

The repository also lists a very small “route 1” that any user can run on a modest machine: building the verifier and checking a stored example proof. The script `verifier/build.sh` is the entry point. When executed from the repository root as a non-root user, the script silently compiles `cp_verify` for about one to two minutes, then prints a line that starts with THE VERIFIER IS BUILT: and exits with code 0.

A warning line that begins with `build.sh: note:` may also appear, but it does not affect the exit status. This quick path lets a reviewer confirm that the proof-checking code works before attempting any of the heavier routes.

## How FlashProve commits and hides model weights

FlashProve separates three stages: commit, prove, and verify. In the commit stage the provider publishes a commitment ID that cryptographically binds to a specific set of model weights. The commitment is a hash-like value; the actual weight tensors never leave the provider’s GPU.

Every subsequent value that depends on the weights is masked, except for a small declared list that the protocol allows to be revealed. This design ensures that anyone who sees the commitment cannot reconstruct the full weight matrix, yet can still trust that later proofs refer to the exact committed model.

The proof generation runs on the provider’s GPU. For each inference request the prover computes a proof that the output token sequence matches what the committed model would produce for the given input. The proof is a succinct arithmetic object that can be streamed to a verifier.

Because the proof is generated on the same hardware that runs the model, the overhead is limited to the 110 tokens / second pre-fill rate reported for Llama 4 Maverick. The source code in `prover/` contains the logic that ties the model’s forward pass to the proof-generation circuit.

## Running the verifier and checking a stored proof

The verification side lives entirely on a CPU. After building `cp_verify` with `verifier/build.sh`, the user runs the binary against a stored example proof that ships with the repository. The verification step completes in under two seconds on a typical x86-64 Linux box with the SHA extensions enabled. The README notes that the verification command prints a success message and returns exit code 0, confirming that the proof matches the commitment ID and the declared list of revealed values.

The script’s output is deliberately minimal. After the silent compile phase, the line `THE VERIFIER IS BUILT:` signals that the binary is ready. Running `./cp_verify example.proof` (the exact command is shown in `README.md`) then produces a line such as `PROOF VERIFIED` before exiting. The source does not provide a numeric benchmark for verification beyond “seconds”, but the described < 2 s runtime gives a concrete expectation for anyone testing the tool on a comparable CPU.

## Performance limits of the different routes

FlashProve defines four execution routes, each with distinct hardware and resource requirements:

1. Verify a stored proof, builds only the verifier, needs < 2 GB RAM, and finishes in 1, 2 minutes for the build plus < 2 seconds for verification. This is the route demonstrated by `verifier/build.sh`.
2. Toy proofs, runs a self-test of the proof library on the CPU, adding `make` and Python 3 to the dependencies. It requires ≤ 1.5 GB RAM and completes in about one minute. This route exercises the same code paths as route 1 but also checks internal consistency.
3. Small model, builds the prover, commits, proves, and verifies an 8-layer synthetic model on a GPU stack. The build needs ~10 GB RAM and takes roughly 29 minutes; the run phase lasts 23, 30 seconds. This route demonstrates end-to-end proof generation on a model far smaller than Llama 4 Maverick but still large enough to stress the GPU pipeline.
4. Full size, replicates the Llama 4 Maverick shape with synthetic weights and a 1,001-token context. The build consumes ~280 GB RAM and about 42 minutes; the prover then runs on an NVIDIA H100 with 80 GB VRAM. The README reports a pre-fill throughput of 110 tokens / second at 24-request batches, confirming that the full-size route is feasible on a single H100.

All GPU-based routes require an x86-64 Linux kernel 4.14 or newer, a CPU with SHA extensions, CUDA 13.2 Update 2 (nvcc 13.2.86) on the PATH, and gcc/g++ 13 as the first compiler in the PATH.

The system must also have at least 330 GB of disk space for the public 4-bit conversion of Llama 4 Maverick (232 GB) plus the calibration set needed for the prover. The repository notes that the only supported platform for the prover is a dedicated H100 that is not shared with other workloads.

## The takeaway

FlashProve separates commitment, proof generation, and verification so that model weights stay hidden while anyone can confirm an inference result in seconds. The quick verifier build (`verifier/build.sh`) lets users validate the proof-checking code on modest hardware before tackling the heavier GPU routes. Understanding the resource profile of each route, especially the RAM and disk demands of the full-size run, helps teams decide whether their machines can safely execute the desired proof workflow.
